titulo: Every sign in Spain that has been lying to you
subtitulo: The words on doors, shutters, platforms and windscreens — read at a glance, with a suitcase in each hand, and acted on before you have translated anything
cena: Ten past one, a glass door with one word painted on it at eye height, three people waiting behind you, and your shoulder is already against the half that does not move.

clique.desconto: Nobody translated a word for you. You read four signs, and the frame you already owned did the rest.
clique.piso: You will read a Spanish street at walking speed and act on it before you have translated it. Most visitors spend a fortnight pushing pull doors.

frasePiso: Spot salida, aseos, empujar and tirar and you are already ahead of most English speakers here — the ones who spend a fortnight pushing pull doors and eating dinner at seven in a place that lives off them.
permissao: You never have to say a single one of these out loud. Reading is the whole job here — and when you get a door back to front, the door tells you in half a second, nobody in the queue thinks anything of it, and everybody standing in it has done the same.
espelho: Standing in the doorway working out which way it opens is the bit that reads as odd there. Everyone else read the word two steps ago and went through without slowing down.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The person ahead of you looks up at the door, reads the word painted on the glass and goes through without breaking step. You look at the handle instead, and push.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: The door is badly made, and anyway a door is a door — I can work it out from the ironmongery like I do at home.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The word is the instruction, and it is doing the entire job. The hardware on a Spanish door is not designed to tell you anything, which is exactly why TIRAR and EMPUJAR are painted at eye height.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Read the four or six letters before your hand arrives. One second, at eye height, every single time.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop being the one person in the doorway going the other way, which is the thing that marks a visitor from ten metres away.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not on the automatic doors of a supermarket, a metro or an airport — there is no word on those and nothing to read, and standing there reading is its own kind of odd.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A Tuesday in August, a whole street of metal shutters down, and one handwritten card taped inside the glass of each.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Something has gone on here — either these places have folded, or I have the day of the week muddled.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The card says the holidays. A family business shuts for the whole month and the card is the only notice there is; the online listing very often still says open.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Read the card, and ring the next place before you walk twenty-five minutes to it.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You plan the week the way the neighbourhood plans it, and August turns into the emptiest, cheapest, longest-evening month you could have picked.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not the big chains, the restaurants or the museums, which stay open all August — and on the coast August is the busiest month of the year, not the quietest.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Three letters on a plate at the edge of the old town, a camera on the post above them, and no barrier, no officer and nothing physically stopping you driving in.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Nothing is blocking the road and nobody is standing there, so this must be advice rather than a rule.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: There is no officer because none is needed. The camera reads the plate and the paperwork travels by post, months later, in Spanish, to wherever you live.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stop before the sign. Leave the car outside the zone and walk in — an old town is a few streets across.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You park once, on the edge, and spend the afternoon on foot in a place that was built before cars and is much better without one.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not every town has a zone — the requirement lands on municipalities over fifty thousand people, so in a village there is no plate, no camera and nothing to read.

steps.pt: Part ten. Warm-up: metronome hand. Sa-li-da. Three taps, all the same size.
Em-pu-jar. Four taps, and the punch lands on the last one. Your mouth will want to move it forward.

steps.promptPt: Yesterday's station, nine minutes to go, and the board has just put a four beside your train that you cannot find on any wall from here. Stop the man in the red waistcoat. Speak now.
steps.pt: the one the board just gave you

steps.es: Vía cuatro es abajo. Pero corre, que el control cierra antes.
steps.pinyin: BEE-ah KWAH-troh es ah-BAH-khoh. PEH-roh KOH-rreh, keh el kon-TROL THYEH-rrah AN-tehs
steps.pt: 👂 'Platform four is downstairs — but hurry, the gate shuts before departure.' — long distance here boards like a small airport.
steps.tts: Vía cuatro es abajo. Pero corre, que el control cierra antes.

steps.pt: Ten past one. A glass door, one word painted on it at eye height, and three people behind you.
Your shoulder is already on it. The word says the other thing, and the door does not move.
Today you say almost nothing. You read, and you act — and the street stops fighting you.
👂 PULL / PUSH — the two that walk you into the door. Read them, then move your hand.
Em-PU-jar is push. Tirar is pull — and it looks like tear, which is the whole of the problem.
Read the word, never the shape of the handle. The ironmongery on a Spanish door tells you nothing.
👂 the way out — and in the plural, over an airport concourse: departures. Follow it on foot, not on a boarding card.
Salida is the way out. It is not a sale — that word is rebajas, and it is the happier one.
At an airport the plural turns it over. Salidas up there means departures, not exits.
👂 toilets, three ways · ground floor. Follow the first three; the fourth is street level, and it is not the button marked 1.
Three words for the toilets, and baño is on none of them. Those three are what is on the door.
Planta baja is the ground floor. The Spanish first floor is one flight up from the street.

steps.promptPt: Third floor of a department store, two coffees ago, and a shop assistant is folding shirts a metre from your elbow. Ask her. Speak now.
steps.pt: the ones with three names
👂 platform · track. Same thing to you, and only one of them is on any given board. Read the one in front of you.
On the metro the platform is the andén. On a Renfe train the same thing is called the vía.
👂 kitchen closed · market price, by weight. First one: the kitchen has stopped, the room has not — sit down and ask what is left. Second one: ask the price per kilo before you order it.
Cocina cerrada means the kitchen has gone home. The room is open, the drinks are on — so ask what is left.
And S.M. beside the fish is según mercado — sold by weight, at today's price. Ask before, not after.

steps.promptPt: Five past five, nothing since the plane, and the only lit place on the street has that card propped in the window. The barman is drying glasses. Speak now.
steps.pt: anything at all, cold, on a plate

steps.es: SOLO EFECTIVO · CON CONVERSIÓN · SIN CONVERSIÓN
steps.pinyin: SOH-loh eh-fek-TEE-boh · kon kon-behr-SYOHN · seen kon-behr-SYOHN
steps.pt: 👂 cash only · with conversion · without conversion. First one: find a machine. The other two are on the card reader, and the one you want is the second.
steps.tts: Solo efectivo. Con conversión. Sin conversión.

steps.pt: Solo efectivo is cash only, and it is perfectly legal here. No bar has to take your card.

steps.promptPt: Saturday, a market stall, half a kilo already on the scale, and the woman has just tapped the little card taped to the till. The man beside you is waiting his turn. Speak now.
steps.pt: somewhere to get money out
The other two live on the little card machine, and the one that shows your own money is the one you do not want.
Sin conversión. Two words. They come back with a number attached in a few parts' time.

steps.es: HAY HOJAS DE RECLAMACIONES A DISPOSICIÓN DEL CONSUMIDOR
steps.pinyin: ai OH-khahs deh rreh-klah-mah-THYOH-nehs ah dees-poh-see-THYOHN del kon-soo-mee-DOR
steps.pt: 👂 complaint forms are available here. Spot it on the wall and remember which wall — it is the poster that makes the form impossible to deny you.
steps.tts: Hay hojas de reclamaciones a disposición del consumidor.

steps.pt: That poster is on the wall behind almost every till in the country, and almost no visitor reads it.
It says the official forms are there. A business that displays it cannot then tell you it has none.

steps.es: NO TOCAR LA FRUTA · FARMACIA DE GUARDIA
steps.pinyin: noh toh-KAR lah FROO-tah · far-MAH-thyah deh GWAR-dhyah
steps.pt: 👂 do not touch the fruit · duty pharmacy. First one: hands in pockets, point. Second one: read the list taped inside the glass — it names the one that is open tonight.
steps.tts: No tocar la fruta. Farmacia de guardia.

steps.pt: At a traditional stall the fruit is hers until it is yours. Hands in your pockets, and point.
And guardia is the word that finds you a chemist at midnight. The rota is on the pharmacy door.

steps.es: HORARIO · HORARIO DE VERANO · CERRADO POR VACACIONES
steps.pinyin: oh-RAH-ryoh · oh-RAH-ryoh deh beh-RAH-noh · theh-RRAH-dhoh por bah-kah-THYOH-nehs
steps.pt: 👂 opening hours · summer opening hours · closed for the holidays. Two ranges, not one — and if a second card is taped over the first, the season on it is the one that counts.
steps.tts: Horario. Horario de verano. Cerrado por vacaciones.

steps.pt: A horario card has two ranges on it, not one. The small shop shuts in the middle of the day.
Roughly half one to half four. The chains, the restaurants and the museums stay open right through it.
Cerrado por vacaciones is August. The family business shuts the month, and the map often has no idea.
GUIRI ALERT. August, thirty-four degrees, and our man has walked twenty-five minutes to a shut door.
There is a card in the glass. He photographs it, sends it to a friend at home, and asks what it says.
Two words. He could have rung ahead. Read the card first — that is the entire trick, the whole fortnight.

steps.es: ZBE · ZONA DE BAJAS EMISIONES · ACCESO RESTRINGIDO · CÁMARAS
steps.pinyin: THEH-tah beh eh · THOH-nah deh BAH-khahs eh-mee-SYOH-nehs · ak-THEH-soh rrehs-treen-KHEE-dhoh · KAH-mah-rahs
steps.pt: 👂 Low-emission zone · restricted access · cameras. Saw it? Don't drive in — park outside and walk.
steps.tts: Zeta, be, e. Zona de bajas emisiones. Acceso restringido. Cámaras.

steps.pt: Three letters on a plate at the edge of an old town, and a camera on the post above them.
Since January twenty twenty-six, every town over fifty thousand people runs one of these zones.
There is nobody standing there. The camera reads the plate, and the envelope reaches your house months later.
Up to two hundred euros, halved if you pay early. And the sticker that lets a car in is only issued in Spain.
So the rule is short, and it works at the speed of a car: see those three letters, and stop before them.

steps.promptPt: Two streets short of the old town, a row of empty spaces along the kerb, and a man is hosing his windscreen at the pump beside you. Point at the row and ask him. Speak now.
steps.pt: here, outside, on this bit of kerb
An old town is a few streets across, and you were going to walk it anyway.
Which leaves one question, and it is the one that turns a fine into a walk. Ask it before the line, not after.
Where can I park without going in?

steps.promptPt: You're two streets short of a sign reading ZBE, there's a petrol station attendant beside you, and you'd rather walk than gamble two hundred euros. Ask where you can park without going in. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where can I park without going in?
👂 not drinking water — on a square fountain. Ask for tap water inside a bar instead: free by law since 2022.
One more on a wall, and it is short. If the fountain says that, fill your bottle somewhere else.
👂 Catalan: open · shut · way out. Same three jobs, different letters. Read them and walk on.
In Barcelona the shutter may say it in Catalan. Obert is open, tancat is shut, sortida is the way out.
Three words you will never say. There is a whole part on that language much later on.
Now watch the person in front of you at the next glass door. Their eyes go up before their hand goes out.
That one second of reading is what stops the doorway collision, and the collision is what marks you.
Not at a supermarket, mind — those doors carry no word and open themselves. Nothing to read there.
You never have to say one of these out loud. Reading is the job, and the door answers in half a second.
Get one back to front and nobody notices but you. Everybody in that queue has done exactly the same.
Count where you spoke, not where you read. The station. The department store. A market stall. An old town.
Nobody translated a word for you. You read four signs, and the frame you already owned did the rest.
Shadowing, and it is short today. Two you will actually say out loud, over the top of them.
Where are the toilets?
Can I leave the car here?
One more out loud, at a door we have not stood at yet. Terminal two, and every board overhead is plural.

steps.promptPt: Case in hand, you want the taxi rank, and every sign above your head is pointing at aeroplanes. There is a woman at the information desk. Speak now.
steps.pt: on foot, into the city
Spot salida, aseos, empujar and tirar, and you are ahead of most English speakers in the country.
That is it. No exam, nothing to write down, and the street stops arguing with you. Hasta luego.

secoes.corpo: SALIDA is the way out and never a sale; the sale is REBAJAS, and the official seasons are January and July. ENTRADA is both the entrance and the admission ticket. EMPUJAR is push and TIRAR is pull — em-PU-jar carries the mnemonic, and between them they cause the daily doorway collision. The toilets are ASEOS, SERVICIOS or LAVABOS; ask for the baño and you will be understood and instantly placed. CABALLEROS and SEÑORAS are gents and ladies, and modern bars also use M/H or ELLOS/ELLAS. ABIERTO and CERRADO are open and closed. PLANTA BAJA, sometimes just PB or 0, is the ground floor, which matters most to Americans: the Spanish first floor is one flight up from the street, so a lift button marked 1 does not take you out. NO FUNCIONA, FUERA DE SERVICIO and AVERIADO all mean out of order. PROHIBIDO EL PASO and PRIVADO mean no entry. CUIDADO CON EL ESCALÓN is mind the step, and it is usually there because the step is a bad one. AGUA NO POTABLE is on square fountains and means exactly what it says.

exemplos.pt: tee-RAR · em-poo-KHAR — pull · push. The one that looks like 'tear' is the one that means pull.
PLAN-tah BAH-khah — ground floor. The button you want in the lift is often 0 or PB, not 1.

secoes.titulo: Platforms, tracks and the door that does not open itself
secoes.corpo: ANDÉN is the platform on the metro; VÍA is the track number on Renfe. They are the same thing from where you are standing, and only one of them will be on the board in front of you. LLEGADAS and SALIDAS are arrivals and departures — the plural of the word that means 'exit' everywhere else in the country, which is the single most reliable false friend in Spain. CERCANÍAS, called RODALIES in Catalonia, is the commuter rail: a separate system with separate tickets, and the airport supplement is separate again. CORRESPONDENCIA and TRANSBORDO both mean interchange. TAQUILLA is the ticket office, VALIDAR is validate and RECARGA is top up. Two that are buttons rather than information: SOLICITE PARADA on a bus means request stop, and if you do not press it the bus does not stop; PULSE PARA ABRIR on a train means press to open, because on many Cercanías and older metro trains the door genuinely will not open by itself and people have watched their station go past waiting for it.

exemplos.pt: POOL-seh PAH-rah ah-BREER — press to open. The door is waiting for you, not the other way round.

secoes.titulo: Money, the counter and the poster nobody reads
secoes.corpo: SOLO EFECTIVO means cash only, and it is entirely legal: there is no obligation in Spain to accept a card, which is why the cash machine is part of the first hour of the trip. On the card reader itself, CON CONVERSIÓN and SIN CONVERSIÓN — or a screen offering you the total in pounds or dollars instead of euros — are the same decision wearing two coats, and the option that shows you your own money is the expensive one. That gets a part of its own later, with the numbers attached. COCINA CERRADA means the kitchen has shut for the gap between services, and drinks carry on. S.M. or SEGÚN MERCADO next to shellfish and fish means the price is by weight at today's market rate, so the question to ask is the price per kilo and the weight of the piece, before it is cooked. MENÚ DEL DÍA is the weekday set lunch; PLATO DEL DÍA is one dish and not the same offer. And HAY HOJAS DE RECLAMACIONES A DISPOSICIÓN DEL CONSUMIDOR is the small framed poster you have walked past a hundred times: the complaint forms are official, they come in three copies, one of which goes to the regional consumer authority, and a business displaying that poster cannot then tell you it does not have any. Refusing to hand one over is itself an offence, separate from whatever the argument was about.

exemplos.pt: SOH-loh eh-fek-TEE-boh — cash only. Legal, common, and the reason to know where the cash machine is.
seh-GOON mehr-KAH-dhoh — market price, by weight. Ask price per kilo and weight before you order.

secoes.titulo: The clock on the shutter: HORARIO, the middle of the day, and August
secoes.corpo: A HORARIO card usually has two ranges on it and not one, because the small shop closes in the middle of the day — roughly ten until half one or two, then again from half four or five until eight or half eight. What does not close: the big chains and supermarkets, the restaurants, which are at their busiest then, and the museums. HORARIO DE VERANO is the summer version of the same card, and where a second card is taped over the first, the season written on it is the one that applies. CERRADO POR VACACIONES means closed for the holidays and in practice means August: a family business shuts for the whole month, the online listing very often still says open, and the honest action is to ring before you walk twenty-five minutes across a city in thirty-four degrees. CERRADO POR DESCANSO DEL PERSONAL is the weekly rest day, usually Sunday or Monday. And FARMACIA DE GUARDIA is the one that saves a night: every locality always has at least one pharmacy on duty outside shop hours, and the rota is posted on the door of every pharmacy — including the dark, shut one you are standing in front of at half eleven at night. The word to look for is guardia.

exemplos.pt: theh-RRAH-dhoh por bah-kah-THYOH-nehs — closed for the holidays. It is August, not a closure.
far-MAH-thyah deh GWAR-dhyah — duty pharmacy. The list of tonight's is taped to the door of the shut one.

secoes.titulo: ZBE: the plate on the road that photographs you
secoes.corpo: Since 1 January 2026 every Spanish municipality over fifty thousand inhabitants, plus the island territories and smaller towns over the pollution limits, has been required to run a low-emission zone — a zona de bajas emisiones, ZBE. They already cover a large share of the population and are still spreading, and they sit exactly where the historic centre is, which is exactly where the hotel is. Enforcement is an automatic camera that reads and traces foreign plates; the fine is classed as a serious infringement, up to €200, reduced to €100 for early payment, with no licence points. The structural trap is the sticker: the DGT environmental label is only issued to vehicles registered in Spain, so a British-plated car cannot simply buy one — a driver bringing their own car down through France has to register it online with each individual city before entering, which is usually free. A car hired in Spain has Spanish plates and a sticker already, so the question there is not whether it has one but which category it is, and that is a thirty-second question to ask at the counter while the person is still in front of you. Either way, the sign on the road is the last chance to decide: see ZBE, stop before it, leave the car outside and walk in.

exemplos.pt: Low-emission zone · restricted access · cameras. Do not drive in to check.
PWEH-dhoh ah-par-KAR ah-KEE — Can I leave the car here? Asked outside the zone, not inside it.

secoes.titulo: When the sign is not in Spanish at all
secoes.corpo: In a neighbourhood bar in Barcelona, Girona, València, Palma, Bilbao or Santiago the menu and the sign may be in the co-official language only, and there is nothing to do about that except recognise a handful of words. Catalan: obert and tancat for open and closed, sortida for the way out, entrada, lavabos or serveis for the toilets, estirar and empènyer for pull and push, esmorzar, dinar and sopar for breakfast, lunch and dinner, preu for price, pa for bread and aigua for water. Basque: irteera for the way out, komuna for the toilet, itxita for closed. Galician: saída, aberto, pechado. You do not need to produce a single one of them, and nobody expects you to. There is a whole part later on what those languages are, what they are not, and the half-dozen courtesy words that visibly change how you are served.

exemplos.pt: oh-BEHRT · tan-KAT — Catalan for open and closed, respelled the way the Spanish voice reads it out in this part.
Catalan for pull and push. Same doorway, different letters — and these two you only ever read, so there is nothing to imitate.
